title: Risk of Large-Scale War Rising — UN Report
paragraphs: The threat of a large-scale war has risen sharply in the eyes of experts around the world, according to a new report published by the United Nations.

The UN Global Risk Report 2026, released in September, is based on the views of about 1,300 people working in government, international organizations, civil society, business and academia across every region of the world. Respondents assessed 28 political, economic, environmental, social and technological threats, considering how likely each one was, how much damage it could cause, and how well prepared the world is to deal with it.

The most striking finding concerned large-scale war, which climbed 16 places in the rankings compared with the previous survey in 2024. This was the steepest rise of any risk on the list. Some 36% of respondents believe a large-scale war could affect a significant share of humanity within a year, while 76% expect this to happen within seven years. It was also the only risk to rank in the top six on all four of the report's measures.

The concern is shared across the globe. Large-scale war and geopolitical tension now rank among the top 10 risks in all seven regions covered by the survey, and in the top five in six of them. Just two years ago, they were in the top five in only one region.

Respondents identified several factors that could increase tensions between countries, including shortages of natural resources, economic fragmentation, misinformation and the weakening of international institutions. In fact, the survey found that the connection between geopolitical tension and war was the strongest of the 705 links it identified between different risks.

War is not the only concern, however. Inaction on climate change was rated the most important risk overall. Meanwhile, risks related to artificial intelligence entered the top 10 in Europe and North America.

In his foreword to the report, UN Secretary-General António Guterres described the findings as "sobering." Guterres noted that the institutions expected to respond to these threats are seen as less able to act. However, the Secretary-General ended with a message of hope: "The choice is ours."
The UN stressed that the report reflects how people perceive risks, rather than predicting the future.
